# The AI-Assisted Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** George E. P. Box originally applied this aphorism to statistical models. Because every model simplifies reality, our working question is always whether that simplification still serves the decision at hand. Whether we build a task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite, we inevitably leave something out. Each tool remains deeply useful provided we understand its scope and ensure our decisions do not overreach the evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
AI can generate more candidates and invoke more tools than any architect can manually inspect. We must organize our work so promising outputs become defensible design decisions rather than a massive pile of plausible results.
:::

As systems architects, we constantly blend explicit artifacts with tacit knowledge [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. While our requirements, models, and review notes capture much of the design, we supply the rest directly from memory. AI assistance dramatically accelerates our exploration across every system stack layer. Generative models quickly propose hundreds of heterogeneous subsystem candidates. However, automated tools can subtly shift the research question, submit invalid microarchitectural configurations, or accept a clean tool exit that measured absolutely nothing. They might optimize a misleading proxy metric [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement] or stretch a result beyond its generating conditions. If we rely solely on a raw sequence of prompts and tool invocations, we lose visibility into where these failures occur.

Because each pitfall demands a different repair, we must organize workflows to catch errors early. Established systems engineering processes divide iterative technical work, enabling teams to review progress and backtrack to whichever step needs revision [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook]. We apply that foundational principle here. We must settle our core architectural question before we judge any generated candidates. Our tools must run successfully before we can evaluate their measurements. We must thoroughly understand checked results before they support a final decision. Accordingly, our workflow moves fluidly through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide. We view each phase as asking a distinct question and leaving a concrete result for the next architect to review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can achieve the following objectives. We contrast ad hoc AI prompts with rigorous architecture methods across hardware and software subsystems. We define the six life-cycle responsibilities, outputs, and targeted repair paths. We manage iterative design loops without relying on rigid waterfall schedules. We distinguish a complete life cycle, scoped study, design loop, and study record. We preserve design context to keep all evidence, tool executions, and failures reviewable.
:::

## Common Pitfalls

Applying unconstrained AI prompts to complex architecture studies without formal lifecycle boundaries introduces severe operational risks. As design teams scale automated generation across System-on-Chip (SoC) components, ad hoc prompting without versioned contracts or structured records triggers recurring failure modes across the hardware-software stack.

**Amplifying an Unverified Baseline Across Stages.** Running thousands of candidate sweeps against an unverified baseline microarchitecture propagates initial modeling errors across every downstream stage. Gathering massive simulation volumes from an uncalibrated baseline yields high-confidence data for a fundamentally invalid architectural comparison.

**Bypassing Versioned Hardware-Software Contracts.** Automated agents often generate hardware blocks or ISA extensions against unversioned software dependencies, unstated ABI constraints, or informal memory interface rules. AI generators naturally optimize candidates against isolated functional checks while ignoring system-level contracts like AMBA Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) interconnect handshakes, Unified Power Format (UPF) power intent, or compiler target flags.

**Optimizing Simulator Loopholes Over Physical Reality.** Learned optimizers frequently exploit measurement artifacts or high-level abstraction gaps in simulation tools. These algorithms ruthlessly maximize reward functions by selecting configurations that exploit simulator timing flaws or missing wire-delay models, producing candidate architectures that fail during gate-level synthesis [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData].

**Skipping Stage-Gated Repair Paths.** Design teams often treat the six-stage lifecycle as an unmonitored pipeline rather than enforcing explicit stage seams. When an evaluation fails or an execution fails to launch, resetting the entire study back to initial formulation discards valid exploration history and wastes compute budgets.

**Operating Without Operational Attempt Records.** Teams frequently invoke automated tools and generative agents without capturing immutable Operational Attempt Records. Running ad hoc prompt loops without logging tool inputs, seed values, environment flags, and raw stderr outputs creates uninspectable shadow state, preventing independent architects from auditing or reproducing claimed architectural results.

Simulation and electronic design automation (EDA) runs are incredibly expensive. A poorly framed question can burn through hundreds of compute hours before we realize our results cannot support a sound design decision.

Software engineering provides a useful comparison. SWE-bench strictly bounds a software task by pairing a repository issue with a known state and executable tests [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. We need that same discipline in architecture. Unlike pure software development, we lack a single test that can simultaneously resolve performance, power, area, timing, physical feasibility, and system-level trade-offs. Instead, we pull relevant feedback from a wide array of specialized tools. It remains an open question whether our Lighthouse reference architecture benchmark could evolve into a multi-fidelity benchmark capable of measuring AI assistance on equal footing. Section @sec-what-architect-owns details exactly what such a benchmark would require.

Ultimately, we have to declare comparability study by study. Consider two teams analyzing the exact same system trade-off. One team might choose `gem5`, a modular simulator built on a discrete-event platform, while the other relies on `FireSim`, an FPGA-accelerated full-system RTL platform [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Either team can successfully compare subsystem throughput and execution times. If we want energy estimates or physical area metrics, we must attach a separate model and state our underlying assumptions. Simply picking a tool does not tell us which workload phases we count or whether we faithfully reran the same baseline. Explicit declarations dictate whether our two teams performed the identical study. As architects working alongside automated methods, we must carry these declarations clearly through candidate selection, tool requests, execution, and verification checks.

## Six Core Responsibilities {#sec-arch2-ontology}

How does partitioning the AI-assisted design lifecycle into six core responsibilities isolate failure domains and target architectural repairs? When we repair a bad question, we take a fundamentally different path than when we fix an illegal candidate or an invalid comparison. We route unsupported explanations and incomplete decisions to completely different places. These distinct repair paths give our six core responsibilities their fundamental purpose. Each responsibility keeps a specific type of failure attached to the job that can fix it.

1. **Formulate** translates design intent into a crisp question, concrete requirements, objectives, legal changes, planned checks, and an intended decision across hardware and software boundaries.
2. **Explore** identifies the alternatives worth testing across coupled subsystem spaces and preserves enough search history to show exactly what we considered.
3. **Implement** makes our candidate executable by the relevant tools and proves the requested work actually ran.
4. **Evaluate** compares valid measurements against the requirements and objectives declared up front.
5. **Interpret and Explain** determines what our result actually means and whether our proposed mechanism truly accounts for it.
6. **Review and Decide** determines what our accumulated work supports, allowing us to advance, reject, revise, or cleanly stop the effort.

To ground these responsibilities, we examine an integrated mobile XR SoC design effort. In an XR platform targeting real-time spatial tracking under a strict 3\ W Thermal Design Power (TDP) envelope, architectural interventions systematically span all eight layers of the prompt stack:
1. **Workload:** We select benchmark traces from `XRBench` (an extended-reality workload suite), Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation (`SPEC2026`) general compute benchmarks, and `MLPerf` machine learning benchmark suites.
2. **ISA and ABI contract:** We enforce the RV64GCV standard and application binary interface rules across vector extensions.
3. **Compute organization:** We evaluate CPU core microarchitecture parameters like out-of-order queue depths alongside Neural Processing Unit (NPU) matrix accelerators and specialized SoC blocks.
4. **Memory and data movement:** We optimize cache hierarchies (L1/L2/L3/TCM), AMBA AXI5 interconnect topologies, NoC bisection bandwidth, and LPDDR5X DRAM timing parameters.
5. **Power envelope:** We enforce passive cooling boundaries and skin-temperature limits under the 3\ W TDP ceiling.
6. **Compiler and runtime stack:** We adjust software translation paths using `Triton` (a domain-specific compiler language), `LLVM` (a modular compiler infrastructure), `MLIR` (a multi-level intermediate representation framework), `TVM`, and domain libraries.
7. **Physical constraints:** We evaluate cell libraries, voltage margins, and area constraints in TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class LP mobile process nodes.
8. **Reliability and verification:** We mandate SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for interface compliance, Unified Power Format (UPF) power-gating intent, and Static Timing Analysis (STA) signoff.

Every handoff carries a distinct, tangible result forward. When that result falls short, the return path routes our work back to the exact responsibility that can repair it (@fig-ontology-loop). This targeted routing carries our design intent toward a reviewed next action without forcing us to restart the study from scratch.

![**Our six-stage life cycle carries design intent to a reviewed decision.** Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide describe our complete set of responsibilities. When we encounter an inadequate result, we return the work directly to the responsibility that owns the fix.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered responsibilities arranged in two rows. A return path shows that review can revise the question, while our other repairs return the work to the specific responsibility that owns the inadequate output."}

In one complete pass, we convert design intent into a scoped plan, legal candidates, executed tool work, checked results, a supported account, and a reviewed next action. We treat the return path as a targeted revision rather than a universal loop back to the beginning. Rapid iteration can easily blur the scale of our work, so we use four specific terms to distinguish our complete effort from the parts that constantly repeat.

- **Life cycle.** Names the complete set of responsibilities we need to move from intent to a defensible decision.
- **Scoped study.** Applies those exact responsibilities to one specific architecture question and one intended decision.
- **Design loop.** Describes our iterative path through the relevant responsibilities as our design changes and feedback returns.
- **Study record.** Preserves our core question, attempts, observations, conclusions, and unresolved issues so another architect can thoroughly inspect our work.

This clear distinction determines exactly what we can reuse and what we must redo. For example, if our baseline simulation result used an obsolete memory model, our scoped study still defines the core question. Our design loop routes the comparison back to the specific work needing repetition, and our study record preserves exactly why the old result no longer applies.

A stage boundary proves genuinely useful when the work on either side can fail independently and requires a distinct repair strategy. We recognize five adjacent boundaries that meet this strict criterion (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Boundary** | **Different questions and outputs** | **Different inadequacy and repair** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate to Explore | Formulate asks what decision our study might support. Explore asks which alternatives fit inside that plan. | We route an inadequate plan back to our question. We route an inadequate exploration back to our legal design space. |
| Explore to Implement | Explore asks which candidate we should try. Implement asks whether we can express that candidate as a valid tool request. | We route an illegal candidate back to our design space. We route a malformed request back to our tool setup. |
| Implement to Evaluate | Implement produces a valid execution record. Evaluate produces our checked comparison. | A run that never executed cannot count against our candidate. A completed run that fails our declared check certainly can. |
| Evaluate to Interpret and Explain | Evaluate asks whether our measured result meets declared requirements. Interpretation asks what our result means. | We route a measurement problem back to our measurement plan. We route a mechanism problem back to our hypothesis. |
| Interpret and Explain to Review and Decide | Interpretation produces our supported account. Review asks what that account permits us to conclude. | We route an incomplete explanation back to our study. An insufficient study record forces us to narrow our conclusion. |

: **Our stage boundaries separate different questions and repairs.** Each row separates work that can fail independently and requires a unique repair strategy. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[20,41,39]"}

Each responsibility needs enough clear information for us to judge its result, inspect exactly what happened, and quickly identify the correct repair when the outcome is inadequate. Formulation naturally comes first because our legal alternatives must exist before exploration can propose candidates.

## The Six Life-Cycle Stages

How do explicit life-cycle stages govern the progression of architectural candidates from initial intent to authoritative decisions? Systematic design automation requires structuring the architecture lifecycle into explicit, repeatable phases. We organize the process into six distinct stages that govern how architectural ideas progress from initial formulation to verified decision handoffs. The following subsections define these stages and elevate their core mechanisms into seminal principles.

### Stage 1 Formulating Core Architecture Questions

We begin formulation with intent, though intent alone rarely provides a testable architecture problem. A system-level goal must translate into concrete workload requirements, architecture choices, and strict interface obligations across subsystems. Handoffs from formulation to exploration formalize component metadata, bus interfaces, register maps, and memory-mapped address spaces using machine-readable IP-XACT (IEEE 1685) schemas. When we define a hardware-software interface, we constrain what software can safely assume and what hardware must reliably provide. Every step of this refinement adds necessary detail without changing the original goal.

Before we choose a search method, our plan must lock in the comparator, the legal changes, the checks, the budget, the stopping conditions, and the intended decision (@tbl-bounded-study-contract). We use hard constraints to rule out a candidate unequivocally. An objective allows us to rank candidates that remain feasible. Clear declarations allow our Explore phase to return the Pareto set of feasible alternatives where we cannot improve one objective without worsening another. We embrace this approach to preserve necessary tradeoffs rather than falsely declaring a single universal winner [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

| **Declaration** | **Prospective mobile XR SoC subsystem study** |
| --- | --- |
| **Question** | Which 3 MiB and 4 MiB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| **Comparator** | The current 2 MiB baseline. |
| **Scope** | One subsystem capacity decision inside the XR compute block. |
| **Permitted changes** | L2 capacity and associated NPU tile buffer partitioning may take values 2 MiB, 3 MiB, or 4 MiB. |
| **Hard constraints** | Modeled subsystem power must not exceed 3\ W. The SRAM macro must not exceed 1.5 square millimeters and its access time must not exceed 2.5\ ns. |
| **Objectives** | Reduce 99th-percentile frame time while limiting added power and area. |
| **Conditions** | A versioned XRBench workload snapshot alongside SPEC2026 and MLPerf traces, an RV64GCV RISC-V software image compiled via Triton, LLVM, or MLIR, and recorded tool versions. |
| **Planned checks** | Run the functional regression suite in `Verilator` (an open-source C++ SystemVerilog simulator) and measure 99th-percentile frame time in `gem5` (a modular cycle-accurate architectural simulator) and `SCALE-Sim` (a cycle-accurate systolic array memory simulator). |
| **Budget** | Four cycle-level execution sweeps in total. |
| **Stopping conditions** | Stop when the intended decision is resolved or the run budget is spent. |
| **Intended decision** | Recommend at most one subsystem capacity configuration for a later gate-level RTL study. |
| **Exclusions** | Subsystem clock domain changes, prefetching algorithms, thermal signoff, and product-level cost. |

: **A scoped plan declares our multi-subsystem comparison before we choose a method.** The question and legal design space determine requirements and planned observations. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Ultimately, an architectural claim makes our expected result falsifiable.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim states the proposed mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives, requirements, and evidence that would count against it.

Our claim forces us to make the connection between mechanism and system-level outcome something our multi-tool measurements must test. As our study proceeds, we must keep all requirements rigorously traceable. A 3\ W limit only becomes operational when we name our units and conditions and explicitly assign the validation check at the consuming interface.

### Stage 2 Exploring Alternatives

We ask which alternatives are worth testing inside the declared legal design space. Our intended decision, represented space, and available budget determine how much exploration is enough. Our exploration record should expose which boundary cases we examined, which regions we pruned using an established check, and what remains unexplored. We must state whether this work supports our intended decision or merely nominates candidates for later testing. If we find an illegal candidate or conduct an inadequate search, we return to the declared legal design space rather than passing the problem to implementation.

Legal does not mean independent. Increasing capacity in one subsystem can alter access time, banking, interconnect distance, leakage, floorplan pressure, and the software-visible benefit of another optimization. We explore coupled alternatives rather than grabbing from a bag of unrelated parameters across CPU cores, NPUs, memory, and software compilers. We record why we sampled or pruned each region and which dependency drove that choice. If a coupling changes a declared workload, interface, constraint, or legal action, the study returns to formulation.

### Stage 3 Implementing Testable Representations

When we implement a selected candidate, we make it executable by our intended tools. Transaction-level interconnect handoffs between IP blocks rely on SystemC TLM-2.0 (Transaction-Level Modeling) socket and generic payload schemas to model memory-mapped bus transactions across heterogeneous subsystems. We define an *Operational Attempt Record* as the immutable, structured audit log generated for every tool execution attempt, joining authorized requests, backend scheduler jobs, input parameters, execution status, returned artifacts, realized computational costs, and terminal failure causes into a single inspectable object. Every time we issue a tool request, we must preserve this record along with both the candidate identity and the overall study state across our heterogeneous tool suite.

We must confirm that each tool actually used our requested parameters. A syntactically valid configuration can easily deceive us by selecting the wrong top-level module or skipping the precise workload region that defines our comparison. This reality highlights a crucial distinction between an infrastructure failure and a candidate failure. If a simulator crashes or a script is malformed, we only know that our requested test failed to run correctly. These glitches tell us absolutely nothing about the quality of our architectural candidate. Only a valid execution produces a result we can trust to ultimately evaluate or reject a design.

::: {.callout-war-story title="War Story: The Eagle Simulator Disconnect and Zero-Cycle Artifacts"}
**The claim.** In Data General's 32-bit Eagle (Eclipse MV/8000) processor project, early microcode simulation runs reported zero-cycle latency and optimal execution across complex instruction routines [@Kidder1981SoulOfANewMachine].

**The gap.** As Tracy Kidder documented in *The Soul of a New Machine*, the microcode simulator passed an uninitialized bus control flag and omitted memory arbitration queueing under load [@Kidder1981SoulOfANewMachine]. Simulation completed instantaneously because downstream log parsers substituted default zeros for unsimulated memory wait states.

**The lesson.** We must recognize zero-latency returns as infrastructure execution failures rather than microarchitectural breakthroughs. A rigorous implementation check confirms that clock models, bus handshakes, and memory requests exist before our evaluation interprets returned metrics.
:::



### Stage 4 Evaluating Candidate Evidence

We can evaluate a candidate only after checking our implementation record to confirm the intended work actually ran. Once verified, we compare returned measurements against the requirements, objectives, and validity conditions we established during formulation. The outcome explicitly details which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, showing precisely how much confidence our measurements justify.

As we shape our order of evaluation, we balance tool cost and fidelity across a multi-fidelity evaluation spectrum spanning all eight layers (@fig-eval-fidelity-latency). Handoffs to physical signoff exchange cell timing, dynamic power, leakage, and pin capacitance tables via Liberty (`.lib`) library schemas for TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class LP mobile nodes. Architectural simulation runs in `gem5` report cycle counts, cache miss ratios, NoC bisection bandwidth congestion, and memory queueing latencies under strict DRAM timing parameters. Fast CACTI SRAM models filter out candidates violating physical area bounds. Integrated runs using `SCALE-Sim`, `gem5`, and `Ramulator` capture dynamic queueing and frame-time latency over millions of cycles under XRBench, SPEC2026, and MLPerf workloads. High-speed SystemVerilog simulation in `Verilator` verifies bit-exact functional correctness and SVA protocol assertions. Gate-level simulation in commercial `VCS` paired with static timing signoff (STA) and power signoff (UPF) tools extracts true dynamic power under gate-level switching activity within our 3\ W TDP target.

```{python}
#| label: fig-eval-fidelity-latency
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Evaluation tool fidelity versus turn-around latency across life-cycle stages.** Early analytical models (SCALE-Sim, Timeloop) yield rapid feedback (~1 ms to 100 ms) with moderate physical fidelity, while full physical signoff (OpenROAD, Cadence, Synopsys Formality) requires hours to days per candidate to reach physical accuracy.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot showing physical and architectural fidelity (0.25 to 1.0) versus turn-around latency per candidate (1 ms to 1 day log scale) across analytical models, gem5, Verilator, FireSim, and Cadence/Synopsys EDA flows."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
import numpy as np

apply_style()

tools = [
    {"name": "Analytical / roofline", "latency": 0.001, "fidelity": 0.35, "color": COLORS["methods"]},
    {"name": "SCALE-Sim / Timeloop", "latency": 0.1, "fidelity": 0.62, "color": COLORS["methods"]},
    {"name": "gem5 / Spike", "latency": 15.0, "fidelity": 0.78, "color": COLORS["workload"]},
    {"name": "Verilator C++ Sim", "latency": 180.0, "fidelity": 0.88, "color": COLORS["workload"]},
    {"name": "FireSim (FPGA)", "latency": 1200.0, "fidelity": 0.94, "color": COLORS["evidence"]},
    {"name": "Yosys / OpenROAD", "latency": 7200.0, "fidelity": 0.96, "color": COLORS["evidence"]},
    {"name": "Synopsys / Cadence Signoff", "latency": 86400.0, "fidelity": 0.99, "color": COLORS["constraints"]},
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

latencies = [t["latency"] for t in tools]
fidelities = [t["fidelity"] for t in tools]
colors = [t["color"] for t in tools]

ax.scatter(
    latencies,
    fidelities,
    c=colors,
    s=70,
    zorder=3,
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.9,
)

sorted_idx = np.argsort(latencies)
ax.plot(
    np.array(latencies)[sorted_idx],
    np.array(fidelities)[sorted_idx],
    color=COLORS["ink"],
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.0,
    alpha=0.7,
    zorder=2,
)

offsets = [
    (0.0012, 0.33),
    (0.12, 0.60),
    (18.0, 0.76),
    (220.0, 0.86),
    (1400.0, 0.92),
    (8500.0, 0.97),
    (100000.0, 0.97),
]
for i, t in enumerate(tools):
    ax.text(
        offsets[i][0],
        offsets[i][1],
        t["name"],
        fontsize=5.8,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["ink"],
        va="center",
    )

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(5e-4, 5e5)
ax.set_ylim(0.25, 1.05)

xticks = [1e-3, 1e-1, 10, 3600, 86400]
xtick_labels = ["1 ms", "100 ms", "10 s", "1 hour", "1 day"]
ax.set_xticks(xticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(xtick_labels, fontsize=5.8)

ax.set_title(
    "Evaluation tool fidelity versus turn-around latency",
    fontsize=7.8,
    pad=10,
    fontweight="bold",
    color=COLORS["ink"],
)
ax.set_xlabel("Evaluation latency per candidate (seconds, log scale)", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.set_ylabel("Physical & architectural fidelity (normalized)", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
plt.show()
```

While higher fidelity strengthens our answer to the declared question, it never widens our decision scope. A cycle-level result in `gem5` does not authorize full silicon fabrication if our study only promised a recommendation for gate-level RTL evaluation. Our evaluation can end in several legitimate states. We must keep invalid executions, unresolved comparisons, and rejected candidates fully visible for subsequent review.

### Stage 5 Interpreting Empirical Results

Even if a favorable number clears all declared checks, we might still struggle to explain why the design actually improved. Evaluation establishes whether a result passes basic checks, whereas interpretation tells us what the result means. Explanation tests whether our proposed hardware-software mechanism truly accounts for that outcome.

A larger cache capacity might improve average latency but degrade tail latency due to NoC contention or compiler thread scheduling. We connect measured outcomes to a concrete physical account rather than just telling a plausible story. Simulator loopholes exist across all subsystem domains. An optimizer in `SCALE-Sim` might achieve throughput by omitting weight buffer sync barriers, causing data hazards. A compiler pass in TVM might eliminate vector spill code in simulation by assuming unconstrained register file capacity, failing when compiled for target hardware in `Verilator`.

Improving a metric and proving a mechanism are two entirely different claims. We should choose required observations before we trigger an expensive run. A top-line score cannot recover miss classifications or per-frame histories discarded along the way. While fluent prose can organize our final account, it can never replace the hard measurements that support it.

### Stage 6 Reviewing Decision Handoffs

The review brings our scoped plan and all subsequent work back together. We ask whether we explored the legal alternatives adequately, whether our intended tools successfully ran, and whether our measurements satisfy declared checks. We must verify that our explanation is credible and whether the accumulated work supports our intended decision.

Through review, we might advance one candidate, reject another, or request an entirely new comparison. We may revise the original question, narrow our conclusion, or simply stop because we exhausted our budget. An honest, unresolved result remains a useful outcome provided our study record clearly explains why the question remains open.

When a result is missing, we must know whether to propose another candidate, repair a tool run, collect another measurement, or narrow our decision. That choice depends on what each stage of our responsibility received, what it produced, and where our failed work should return (@tbl-stage-contracts).

| **Stage** | **Receives** | **Produces and checks** | **Repair and handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Formulate** | Product intent, a design question, and known requirements. | A scoped plan whose question, comparator, and exclusions agree. | Repair our question or scope. |
| **Explore** | Our scoped plan and declared legal changes. | One or more legal candidates and their selection history. | Repair our design space or search approach. |
| **Implement** | A candidate, requested tool work, and required inputs. | An execution record showing the requested work ran on our intended state. | Repair our request or tool setup. |
| **Evaluate** | Completed tool returns, planned metrics, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved. | Repair our measurement plan, rerun within budget, or reject the candidate. |
| **Interpret and Explain** | The checked result and proposed mechanism. | An account supported, revised, or contradicted by a direct physical reason. | Repair our hypothesis or request missing observations. |
| **Review and Decide** | The scoped plan and study record. | A decision within the declared scope, a narrower conclusion, or an honest stop. | Reopen the work that owns the missing result or close our study. |

: **Each responsibility produces an artifact we can inspect.** Our inputs, outputs, and repair paths remain distinct. {#tbl-stage-contracts tbl-colwidths="[15,25,34,26]"}

During review, we choose actions solely within our assigned authority. While our system might propose a candidate, it cannot override human judgment. When review calls for revision, we name the responsibility that reopens the task, taking care to preserve the requirements and tool conditions from which the repaired work proceeds.

## Managing Revisions

How do targeted return paths route inadequate outputs back to specific life-cycle responsibilities without corrupting global study state? We do not treat revision as a separate seventh stage. When we produce an inadequate output, we simply return the work to the responsibility that owns the repair. If we generate a malformed tool request for `SCALE-Sim`, we route it back to Implement without altering the candidate itself. When a product requirement changes, we reopen Formulate.

We rely on a design loop to keep each change tightly connected to our original question and our next decision. The path we illustrate in @fig-design-loop shows how our scoped study can revisit the responsibility that owns each repair while preserving valid work.

![**Our design loop revisits the life-cycle responsibility that owns each repair.** We return a named repair to the responsible stage, while we push a supported result toward a scoped outcome.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="82%" fig-alt="Six life-cycle responsibilities shown as our recurrent path through a scoped plan, legal candidate, execution record, checked result, supported account, and next action."}

We start each pass with our current scoped plan and a legal candidate. As we run the tool, we add either an execution record or note an infrastructure failure. We use declared checks to turn valid outputs into a measured result, allowing us to determine exactly what mechanism those measurements support. During Review, we explicitly name our next action. If we find a result inadequate, we record our return path to show which responsibility must act next and why.

When we conduct parallel work, we must rigorously preserve the same study state. We ensure each branch names the specific study revision it used, and we record our actions strictly against that revision. We merge results only after verifying that their assumptions, interfaces, and permitted changes remain perfectly compatible. If we change a shared requirement, we revalidate affected results in all other branches.

We preserve crucial learning by keeping every result permanently attached to its study revision. When a change invalidates a result, we do not erase the data, but we prevent that outdated result from silently carrying forward as current evidence.

## Design-Loop Cards {#sec-design-loop-card}

How do Design-Loop Cards structure and index design state to ensure transparent architectural provenance and accountability? The Design-Loop Card acts as an essential, structured index that binds automated execution data directly to architectural intent and accountability. Rather than prescribing a universal format, this card elevates the preservation of design state, constraints, and failures into a core engineering requirement. It provides a compact index into the specific artifacts that bear on a single, scoped architecture question and the decision our work supports.

We borrow the core reporting instinct behind model cards and datasheets for datasets, tools that make intended use and known limits readily reviewable [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. Because our designs evolve rapidly, our architecture studies must preserve the changing design state, tool conditions, failed checks, and the explicit authority for the next action. A static description of a model simply cannot carry those responsibilities by itself.

To manage these dynamic requirements, we need a study record that makes our architectural state and its revisions fully inspectable.

> **Study record.** The cumulative account of one scoped architecture study. It retains the plan, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the detailed artifacts needed for review or replay.

For every consequential transition, our study record explicitly names the revision. It details exactly who or what proposed and approved the action, what executed it across our tool flows, what checked the result, and what later change might invalidate it. We capture the specific decision being supported, the physical assumptions bounding our results, and the named authority empowered to act on them.

To be truly useful, this index must directly connect our overarching project goals and constraints to our specific comparisons, tool work, returns, findings, and next actions. We establish this critical connection through a scoped study (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl).

![**Our scoped architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study container binds our question and decision to the scope, claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing our architecture intent and judgment above a scoped architecture study container. Returns from all our implementation tools join a common path back to the study."}

While project requirements and overarching rationale set high-level goals, they rarely tell us which specific subsystem capacities we should compare. We use the study question to pinpoint the exact comparison, while our intended decision explains precisely why we are running it. We rely on the scope and architectural claim to declare what our results must test explicitly.

Our study tightly binds our methods and tool returns directly to that claim. We lean on cycle-level simulators to evaluate architectural behavior, while our compilers and runtimes expose critical software interactions, and our RTL generators produce executable implementations. Finally, we turn to RTL and gate-level EDA flows to assess physical properties and exact execution. The returns from all four tool families flow back into our study, allowing us to judge the supported finding against our original question.

We must remember that a raw tool output is not a decision. A supported finding requires explicit limits and a designated owner responsible for the next action. If our results expose a faulty assumption, we step back and deliberately revise our study question or claim. We never allow disconnected tool outputs to blindly stand in for our professional engineering judgment.

We provided our design-loop card in @fig-filled-design-loop-card as an optional, highly compact index into that study record.

![**Our optional study card separates support from decision.** Our cache example connects intent and scope to our methods, checks, results, and rejected alternatives. Its final row keeps what our evidence supports safely separate from the accountable decision.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="84%" fig-alt="Our optional filled study card for the XR capacity comparison. A claim under review appears above entries for the baseline, candidates, failed runs, rejection checks, evidence support, and accountable decision."}

Our claim at the top clearly anchors the specific entries below it. We track the work we planned or already performed in the middle rows, cleanly distinguishing infrastructure failures from legitimately rejected candidates. We reserve the final row to keep our evidence-based support firmly separated from the accountable decision itself. We treat this card as a compact view of our study record rather than a substitute for our carefully linked engineering records.

## Open Questions

What open research questions emerge when scaling structured life-cycle responsibilities across automated multi-agent environments? Our six-stage life cycle succeeds by isolating failures and preserving design intent. Pushing this discipline to production scale surfaces unresolved tensions where human judgment collides with automated volume. The frontier of our research lies exactly in this collision. The following subsections outline these foundational research problems, which remain essential to scaling verifiable automated design.

### Repair and Reviewable State

When our studies encounter multiple failures across different responsibilities, we must decide where to start repairs and which parts of the failed work we should keep around for later review. If we fix the most obvious symptom, like a simulator crash in `SCALE-Sim`, we risk triggering another expensive invalid run while deeper issues remain untouched. We need principled ways to judge what we should retain, balancing the cost of review against the value of documenting the conditions that triggered our failures.

### Proportionate Structure and Independent Review

We need a life cycle that catches silent drift in our design questions and ensures credible review without demanding tapeout-level rigor for every early-stage exploration. As we move from defining goals to running RTL flows in `Verilator`, our workload constraints or acceptance conditions can slowly drift. We need mechanisms to spot material shifts early without forcing us to restart the entire study. Furthermore, we face a critical challenge when reviewing a study where the same AI proposed the candidates, ran the measurements, and wrote the explanation. We must define which responsibility boundaries truly need independent verification or human decision rights.

## Conclusion

How does an explicit six-stage life cycle transform chaotic AI candidate generation into verifiable architectural decisions?

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains to enable targeted repair"}
**Principle.** We must structure our AI-assisted design life cycle so that independently failing outputs belong to distinct responsibilities.

**Rationale.** When our components fail independently, we must keep their repairs cleanly decoupled.

**Action.** Route any inadequate result directly back to the responsibility that owns its repair. We must preserve our original design questions, selected candidates, tool configurations, and valid prior results to prevent redundant computation and state corruption.
:::

Our AI-assisted design life cycle keeps the entire path from our initial intent to a reviewed architecture decision highly coherent. As architects, we turn a broad goal into testable requirements, objectives, legal alternatives, and an intended decision. We find candidates inside that space. Our simulators, compilers, RTL flows, and gate-level EDA tools make those candidates testable, while execution checks help us separate valid work from infrastructure failure. Declared checks qualify our results, and we connect them directly to an architectural mechanism and its limits before deciding whether to advance, reject, revise, or stop.

We treat these responsibilities as an adaptable framework rather than a rigid waterfall or black-box agent architecture. We repeat, overlap, and return to them whenever our work needs repair. We design this process to prevent different failures from collapsing into a single unsuccessful run. A malformed tool invocation is not a rejected design. A favorable score is not a substitute for an explanation. A higher-fidelity measurement does not grant broader authority, and a budget stop is never a completed decision.

In our XR subsystem example, we saw how a tightly scoped study uses this complete life cycle. We translated our broad system goal into a narrow decision about which subsystem capacity we should advance to gate-level RTL evaluation. We kept hard constraints strictly separate from tradeoff objectives, and we ensured our tail latency stayed connected to real-time workload deadlines. Before any single metric could reject a candidate, our tool requests had to establish that the intended design actually ran. Our final study record preserved our open questions and decision limits up front.

Bringing AI assistance into our workflows increases the need to preserve our design intent as our work crosses models, methods, software, hardware descriptions, simulators, and physical tools. This life cycle gives us a common structure for those handoffs. We can push more work forward without letting the speed or fluency of the system substitute for our own engineering judgment.

That structure operates successfully only when our study has usable data, current project knowledge, and representations that preserve the design relationships our work depends on. We develop those requirements in Section @sec-data-representations-world-models, recognizing that no single representation can serve us across every stage.
